title: Molokhia for the Judges
teaser: Everyone at the cooking competition made fancy food. Ola made her grandmother’s soup.
paragraphs: Ola is twenty-one and works in a hotel kitchen in Sharm El Sheikh. She cuts vegetables and washes plates all day, but she dreams of being a chef. One day, she sees an advert for a cooking competition for young cooks.

The other competitors are very confident. They talk about French sauces, Japanese knives and expensive ingredients. Ola feels small. She does not have expensive things. She only has her grandmother’s recipes in her head.

In the final round, each cook must make one dish that tells their story. The others make beautiful plates with tiny flowers and colourful sauces. Ola makes molokhia with rice and chicken, exactly like her grandmother, with garlic and coriander fried in ghee.
When the judges taste it, the room becomes quiet. One judge, an old chef from Lebanon, closes his eyes. “This tastes like home,” he says. “Simple food is the hardest to cook perfectly.”
Ola does not win first prize. She wins second. But after the competition, the old chef gives her his card. “Come and work in my restaurant in Cairo,” he says. “Bring your grandmother’s recipes.”

title: Why Browned Food Tastes So Good
teaser: Toast, grilled meat and roasted coffee share one chemical secret.
paragraphs: Why does grilled meat taste so much better than boiled meat? Why is toast more delicious than plain bread? The answer is a chemical process called the Maillard reaction, named after the French scientist Louis-Camille Maillard, who described it in 1912.

The Maillard reaction happens when proteins and certain sugars are heated together. It produces hundreds of new flavour and aroma compounds, as well as the brown colour we associate with roasted, grilled and baked food. It is responsible for the crust on bread, the smell of roasting coffee and the deep flavour of fried onions.

It needs relatively high temperatures, usually above 140 degrees Celsius. Water boils at 100 degrees, so food that is wet or boiled cannot brown properly. That is why chefs dry meat before frying it and why overcrowding a pan, which traps steam, gives you grey instead of golden food.

It is different from caramelisation, which happens when sugar alone is heated and breaks down. Both create brown colours and rich flavours, and they often happen together, for example when onions are cooked slowly.

There is a limit, however. If food is heated too long, browning turns into burning, which tastes bitter. Good cooks control the heat and the time carefully, aiming for the moment when the colour is golden brown and the smell makes everyone come to the kitchen.

title: The Foul Truck
teaser: Two friends turned an old van into the best breakfast in Alexandria.
paragraphs: Moataz and Ibrahim are best friends from Alexandria. They both love foul and falafel. Every morning, they eat at the same cart near the sea. One day, Moataz says, “What if we make our own breakfast truck? But different. Modern.”
They buy an old van with their savings. They paint it yellow and blue, like the sea and the sun. Inside, they put a small kitchen. They call it Foul Express.

Their idea is to keep the traditional taste but add new things: foul with tahini and pomegranate, falafel stuffed with cheese, and fresh bread baked every morning. They test the recipes on their families for a month. Ibrahim’s mother is the toughest judge.

On the first day, they park near a university. Students are curious about the colourful truck. A food blogger takes photos and posts a review. “Crispy, fresh and cheap,” he writes. The next morning, there is a long queue.

Now Foul Express has two trucks. Moataz and Ibrahim wake up at four every morning to cook. It is hard, but they love it. And every Friday, they still eat breakfast at the old cart near the sea, where everything began.

title: Why Spicy Food Burns — and Why People Love It
teaser: Chilli is not hot. It just tricks your brain.
paragraphs: When you bite a hot chilli, your mouth feels as if it is on fire, your eyes water and you reach for a drink. But the chilli is not actually hot. The burning feeling comes from a molecule called capsaicin, and it is a clever trick on your nervous system.

Your tongue and mouth have receptors that detect dangerous heat, for example from very hot tea. Capsaicin happens to activate these same receptors. So your brain receives the message “burning!” even though the temperature is normal. Your body reacts as if it were overheating: you sweat, your face turns red and your nose runs.

Plants probably developed capsaicin to protect themselves from mammals, which chew and destroy seeds. Interestingly, birds do not feel the burn, so they happily eat chillies and spread the seeds far away.

Why do humans enjoy this pain? One theory is that the body responds to the burn by releasing endorphins, natural chemicals that reduce pain and can create a pleasant feeling. Another is benign masochism: enjoying a scary or painful experience because we know it is actually safe, similar to riding a roller coaster.

If your mouth is on fire, water is not the best solution, because capsaicin does not dissolve well in it. Milk, yoghurt or a piece of bread works better, which may explain why so many spicy cuisines serve dishes with yoghurt or rice.

title: The Night Train to Aswan
teaser: Rawan travelled alone for the first time. The train had other passengers with stories.
paragraphs: Rawan is twenty-two and lives in Cairo. She has never travelled alone. For her birthday, she buys a ticket for the night train to Aswan. Her mother is worried. “Call me every two hours,” she says.

Rawan shares a small sleeping cabin with an older woman from Nubia called Hajja Aisha. At first, Rawan is shy. But Hajja Aisha offers her dates and tea from a flask, and soon they are talking like old friends.

Hajja Aisha tells her about her village near Aswan: the colourful houses, the Nile, and the old Nubian language that her grandchildren are forgetting. She teaches Rawan a few Nubian words. Rawan writes them in her phone.
In the morning, the train arrives in Aswan. The light is golden and the air is warm. Hajja Aisha says, “You must visit my village. My son has a boat.” Rawan is not sure, but she says yes.

That afternoon, she sits in a boat on the Nile, eating fish with Hajja Aisha’s family. She calls her mother. “Are you OK?” her mother asks. Rawan looks at the river and smiles. “Mama, I’m more than OK.”

title: Why Jet Lag Makes You Feel So Strange
teaser: Your watch changes in a second. Your body takes days.
paragraphs: After a long flight across several time zones, many travellers feel tired at noon and wide awake at three in the morning. They may also feel hungry at strange times, have headaches or find it hard to concentrate. This is jet lag, and it happens because your body has its own internal clock.

Almost every cell in your body follows a roughly 24-hour cycle called a circadian rhythm. A master clock in the brain coordinates these rhythms, controlling when you feel sleepy, when your body temperature rises and falls, and when certain hormones are released.

The most important signal that sets this clock is light. When you fly from Cairo to New York, the local time is seven hours behind, but your internal clock still expects Cairo’s day and night. It can only shift by about an hour or so per day, so it may take nearly a week to fully adjust.
Flying east is usually harder than flying west. Going west makes your day longer, and most people find it easier to stay up later than to fall asleep earlier.

To reduce jet lag, experts suggest getting sunlight in the morning at your destination, avoiding long naps, drinking enough water and eating meals at local times. Some people start shifting their sleep schedule a few days before they travel.

title: The Family Vlog
teaser: The Hassans filmed their holiday. The best part was a mistake.
paragraphs: The Hassan family has a small YouTube channel. Dad films, Mum plans everything, and the three children, Malak, Adam and baby Joury, are the stars. They film their life: birthdays, cooking, and trips around Egypt.
This summer, they go to Marsa Matrouh. Mum has a perfect plan: beach in the morning, lunch at a famous fish restaurant, and a sunset video on the rocks.

Nothing goes to plan. On the first day, it is very windy, and sand gets into everything. The famous restaurant is closed. Adam drops Dad’s phone into the sea. Baby Joury cries for two hours. Mum sits on the hotel bed and says, “This is the worst vlog ever.”

Then Malak has an idea. “Let’s film the problems,” she says. So they do. They film Dad trying to dry his phone in a bowl of rice. They film Mum making sandwiches on the balcony. At night, the wind stops, and they all sit on the beach under the stars.

The video is called “Our Worst Holiday Ever”. It becomes their most popular video. Thousands of families comment with their own funny holiday disasters. Mum learns something: people do not want perfect. They want real.

title: Does Being the Oldest Child Change Your Personality?
teaser: Firstborn, middle child, baby of the family — what science really says.
paragraphs: In many families, people say things like “She is responsible because she is the oldest” or “He is spoiled because he is the youngest”. The idea that birth order shapes personality is very popular. But what does research actually show?

The idea became famous through the Austrian psychologist Alfred Adler in the early twentieth century. He suggested that firstborn children, who once had their parents’ full attention, become responsible and sometimes anxious; middle children feel ignored and become sociable negotiators; and the youngest are charming and rebellious.

For decades, small studies seemed to support these ideas. However, many of them compared siblings within the same family, where older children are, naturally, more mature at the time of the study. When researchers analysed very large samples of thousands of people and controlled for age and family background, most personality differences almost disappeared.

One small but consistent finding remains: firstborns tend to score very slightly higher on intelligence tests, perhaps because they receive more one-to-one time with parents early on. The difference is tiny and says nothing about any individual.

So why does the belief persist? Partly because it is easy to remember examples that confirm it and forget those that do not. And within a family, roles really do matter, even if they do not permanently change who we are.

title: The Cat Who Chose Us
teaser: Nobody in the family wanted a cat. The cat didn’t care.
paragraphs: It is a cold winter night in Heliopolis. A small grey cat is crying under the Saeed family’s car. Omar is twenty-five and still lives with his parents. He wants to bring it inside. His father says no. “We don’t have time for a pet,” he says.

But the next morning, the cat is sitting on their doorstep. And the next. Omar gives it a little milk and some chicken. His mother tells him that cats should drink water, not milk, so he gives it a bowl of water too. The cat starts waiting for Omar every day after work.
One night, there is a big storm. The cat is wet and shaking at the door. Omar’s father opens the door, looks at the cat and sighs. “Only for tonight,” he says.
That night, the cat sleeps on the father’s feet. In the morning, he says nothing. In the evening, he comes home with a cat bed and a bag of cat food. Omar laughs. “Only for tonight, Baba?”

They take the cat to the vet for vaccinations. They name her Ghayma, which means cloud, because she is grey and soft. Now Ghayma has a favourite place in the house: the father’s chair. And the father does not seem to mind at all.

title: Crows Are Smarter Than You Think
teaser: They use tools, recognise faces and remember who was rude to them.
paragraphs: The crows you see on Cairo’s rooftops may look ordinary, but scientists consider crows and their relatives, such as ravens, among the most intelligent animals on Earth. In some tests, they perform at a level similar to young children and great apes.

Some crows use tools. On islands in the Pacific, New Caledonian crows shape sticks and leaves into hooks to pull insects out of holes. In experiments, crows have solved puzzles with several steps, for example dropping stones into a tube of water to raise the level until they can reach floating food.

Crows also remember faces. In a famous study in the United States, researchers wore a specific mask while trapping some crows. Years later, crows in the area still scolded people wearing that mask, even crows that had never been trapped. They seemed to have learned from other crows that the face was dangerous.

They are social and communicate a lot. Crows have many different calls and may gather around a dead crow, possibly to learn about danger in that place. Some people who feed crows regularly report receiving small objects, like buttons or pieces of glass, though scientists are careful about calling these gifts.
Their brains are small, but they are packed with neurons, especially in the areas linked to planning and problem-solving. Crows show that intelligence can evolve in very different bodies.

title: The Balcony Garden
teaser: Old bottles, a broken chair and some seeds. Nada built something beautiful.
paragraphs: Nada lives in a small flat in Mohandessin. Her balcony is grey and empty. There are only some old boxes and a broken chair. One day, she watches a video about gardens made from recycled things. She decides to try.

First, she cleans the balcony. She does not throw away the old things. She cuts plastic bottles in half and makes small holes in the bottom for the water. She paints them in bright colours: yellow, orange and green.
Then she takes the broken chair. She removes the seat and puts a big pot inside the frame. It looks like a strange, beautiful plant stand. She uses the old wooden boxes as shelves.

Now she needs plants. She buys seeds for mint, basil, tomatoes and chillies. Her neighbour, Uncle Mahmoud, gives her some soil and lots of advice. “Water in the morning or evening, never at noon,” he says.

After two months, the balcony is green. The mint is perfect for tea, and the first small tomatoes are red. Nada drinks her morning tea out there every day. Uncle Mahmoud looks at the garden from his window and says, “Next year, you must teach me.”

title: Why Taps Drip — and How to Fix One
teaser: That drip-drip-drip wastes thousands of litres a year. The fix often costs a few pounds.
paragraphs: A dripping tap seems like a small problem, but one drop per second adds up to thousands of litres of water a year. In many cases, the fix is simple and cheap, and you can do it yourself with basic tools.

Most traditional taps work with a rubber washer. When you turn the handle, a screw pushes the washer down onto a seat inside the tap and blocks the water. Over time, the rubber becomes hard, cracked or worn, and water starts to leak through. Modern taps often use ceramic discs instead, but the idea is similar: a seal wears out.

Before starting, turn off the water supply, either under the sink or at the main valve. Then open the tap to let the remaining water out, and put a cloth in the sink so that small parts do not fall into the drain.

Remove the decorative cap on the handle, unscrew the handle, and then use a spanner to loosen the part underneath. Inside, you will find the washer or cartridge. Take the old one to a hardware shop so you can buy exactly the same size, replace it, and put everything back in reverse order.

If the tap still drips, the seat itself may be damaged, or the problem may be elsewhere. At that point, it is wise to call a plumber. But even then, understanding how the tap works helps you explain the problem and avoid paying for unnecessary work.

title: The Sound of Rain
teaser: Ahmed could not sleep for months. Then he found a strange channel.
paragraphs: Ahmed is a nurse in a big hospital in Cairo. He works long night shifts. When he comes home in the morning, he is very tired, but he cannot sleep. The street is noisy, and his mind does not stop.

One morning, a colleague sends him a link to an ASMR video. In the video, a woman whispers softly and taps her fingers on a wooden box. Ahmed thinks it is very strange. But he is so tired that he tries it.
After ten minutes, he feels a soft tingle on his head and neck, and his body relaxes. He does not finish the video. He falls asleep.

Ahmed starts to explore other videos. Some people do not like whispering, and he does not like it every time either. He discovers that his favourite sounds are simple: rain on a window, pages of a book turning and the quiet sound of someone writing with a pencil.

Now, after every night shift, Ahmed puts on his headphones and plays a long video of rain on a roof in a forest. He sleeps for six hours. He tells his colleagues about it, and some of them laugh. But two of them ask him for the link.

title: ASMR: The Tingle Science Is Still Explaining
teaser: Whispers, tapping, crinkling. Why do some brains love them?
paragraphs: ASMR stands for autonomous sensory meridian response, a scientific-sounding name invented online around 2010. It describes a pleasant, tingling feeling that some people experience, usually starting on the scalp and moving down the neck and back, in response to certain gentle sounds or sights.

Common triggers include whispering, soft speaking, tapping on objects, crinkling paper, and slow, careful hand movements. Many popular videos also imitate personal attention, such as someone pretending to cut your hair or examine your eyes.

Not everyone feels it. Surveys suggest that a significant minority of people experience the tingles, while others feel nothing, and some find the sounds irritating. People who experience ASMR often report that it helps them relax, reduces stress and helps them fall asleep.

Scientific research is still young. A few brain-imaging studies found that during ASMR, areas linked to reward and social bonding were more active. One study measured a small drop in heart rate while participants watched ASMR videos, similar to the effect of other relaxation methods.

Some researchers believe ASMR may be connected to the calming feeling of being cared for, like a parent gently grooming a child. Others think it is related to how certain brains process sounds. For now, the best test is simple: if it relaxes you, it works for you.
